plan.topic: Tirzepatide burping and heartburn: how often the label reports belching, reflux and indigestion for each dose vs placebo, why slower stomach emptying can cause them, everyday habits that may help, and the signs that mean seeing a clinician
plan.angle: Keep the angle as written, with these exact fixes: chapter 4 says 'NHS advises not eating within 3 or 4 hours before bed, and raising the head of the bed by around 10 to 20 cm instead of adding pillows'. The NHS trigger list is quoted exactly and framed as 'may trigger it for some people'. Chapter 6 credits to NHS only the triggers its pages actually print. Vomiting blood, black stools and chest pain are untagged urgent signs → 'your local urgent care or emergency number'. 'Sulfur burps' is called a commonly described symptom, with no explanation of the cause.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide Burping and Heartburn: What Helps
plan.why: It's the next unanswered Lane A side-effect question next to the big three. The label rates and NHS guidance can be verified in depth, and holiday meals make it timely. | fact-check: This is a good Lane A topic. Burping (eructation), dyspepsia and GERD are all listed among the Zepbound label's most common adverse reactions (≥5%), so the per-dose vs placebo rates exist. Copy them exactly from the 28 Aug 2026 label table (pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf), keep the pooled-trial population, and don't pool the arms. Three corrections to the angle: (a) The NHS heartburn page (nhs.uk/conditions/heartburn-and-acid-reflux, last reviewed 20 Nov 2023, next review due 20 Nov 2026, so re-check the live date before citing) says 'do not eat within 3 or 4 hours before bed'. It does NOT say 'avoid lying down for 3 hours after eating'. Use the NHS wording or drop the tag. For raising the head of the bed, NHS says 'by around 10 to 20cm, so your chest and head are above your waist' and not to use extra pillows. Credit the trigger foods only as NHS lists them ('coffee, tomatoes, alcohol, chocolate and fatty or spicy foods'), and say these are things that may trigger it for some people, never 'bad' foods. (b) The NHS see-a-GP triggers are heartburn most days, pharmacy medicines not helping, food getting stuck, being sick often, and losing weight for no reason. 'Vomiting blood' and 'black stools' must be found on the NHS indigestion page before they're credited to NHS; otherwise present them as untagged warning signs that need same-day care. Don't use NHS 111 alone; use 'your local urgent care or emergency number'. (c) No source supports anything specific about 'sulfur burps', so call it a commonly described symptom and attach no mechanism. Delayed gastric emptying should be described in label wording, and 'food sitting longer' is a likely explanation, not a proven cause. All the other guardrails in the angle are correct and should stay: the pancreatitis and gallbladder label wording, chest pain → emergency number, the scoped don't-stop line, the hypoglycemia caveat for people on insulin or a sulfonylurea, the pharmacist line with no products, and the prescriber line.

scenes.narration: First, a quick translation. The label uses medical words. Eructation means burping. Dyspepsia means indigestion. And gastroesophageal reflux disease means acid coming back up, which can cause heartburn.

scenes.narration: Burping. On placebo, about one percent of people reported it. On tirzepatide, it was four percent at five milligrams, five percent at ten milligrams, and five percent at fifteen milligrams.

visual.stock_query: bar chart with cartoon burp bubbles

scenes.narration: Indigestion. Four percent on placebo, compared with nine percent at five milligrams, nine percent at ten milligrams, and ten percent at fifteen milligrams.

visual.stock_query: bar chart with cartoon stomach icons

scenes.narration: Reflux. Two percent on placebo, compared with four percent at five milligrams, four percent at ten milligrams, and five percent at fifteen milligrams.

visual.stock_query: bar chart with small flame icons

scenes.narration: So yes, all three were more common on tirzepatide than on placebo. That's why they're on the label's list of most common side effects.

visual.stock_query: label list with three items highlighted

scenes.narration: But flip the numbers around. Even at fifteen milligrams, roughly nine in ten people didn't report indigestion, and about ninety-five in a hundred didn't report burping.

visual.stat_label: Didn't report indigestion, tirzepatide 15 mg, 72-week trials
visual.stock_query: crowd of ten, one holding stomach

scenes.narration: And notice the placebo column. Some people on placebo injections reported indigestion too. Stomachs grumble in everyday life, with or without medicine.

visual.stock_query: two friends both rubbing tummies, smiling

scenes.narration: Imagine Dana, forty-seven, a few weeks into tirzepatide. Her burps aren't in her head. They're real and they're listed, and while most people in the trials didn't report them, she's far from alone.

visual.stock_query: woman in her forties at kitchen table, thoughtful

scenes.narration: But a number only tells you how often. It doesn't tell you why a smaller meal can feel bigger. That's where your stomach's timing comes in.

visual.stock_query: cartoon clock inside a stomach

scenes.narration: The label says it plainly. Tirzepatide delays gastric emptying. In everyday words, food leaves your stomach more slowly.

visual.stock_query: chapter card, friendly stomach, teal gradient

scenes.retention_device: Chapter change with key fact up front

scenes.narration: Think of your stomach as a waiting room with a door at the bottom. Normally the door lets food through at a steady pace. On tirzepatide, that door opens more slowly.

visual.stock_query: stomach as waiting room, slow door

scenes.narration: Food sitting in your stomach for longer is a likely explanation for some of the fullness, pressure and burping people describe. Likely, not proven.

visual.stock_query: calm Medi mascot with question mark

scenes.narration: The idea is that a stomach that stays fuller for longer gives air and acid more chances to travel back up. It's a reasonable explanation, but trials haven't proven it's the cause.

visual.stock_query: cartoon bubbles rising from full stomach

scenes.narration: So what does that mean for Dana's nine o'clock burn? If her stomach is still busy with dinner when she lies down, gravity isn't on her side.

visual.stock_query: woman lying flat in bed, night room

scenes.narration: And then there's the burp with a smell. Some people describe sulfur burps, burps that smell like rotten eggs.

visual.stock_query: person wrinkling nose, cartoon egg

scenes.retention_device: Names the awkward thing viewers search for

scenes.narration: The sources we use don't explain what causes it, so we won't guess. If it's bothering you, or it comes with other symptoms, mention it to your prescriber.

visual.stock_query: friendly chat with prescriber at desk

scenes.narration: One more thing slower emptying affects: medicines you take by mouth. The label says tirzepatide may affect how they're absorbed.

scenes.narration: That matters later, when we talk about pharmacy remedies. Hold that thought.

scenes.narration: Now the part you can actually do something about. These are habits from the NHS guidance on heartburn and acid reflux, plus a few common-sense ones.

visual.stock_query: chapter card, toolkit, green gradient

scenes.narration: First, the NHS suggests eating smaller, more frequent meals. If one big plate feels like too much, splitting it up may ease that full feeling.

visual.stock_query: three small plates instead of one big

scenes.narration: Second, timing. The NHS advises not eating within three or four hours before bed.

visual.stock_query: clock showing early dinner, cosy kitchen

scenes.narration: For Dana, that could mean moving dinner a little earlier, so her stomach has more time before she lies down.

visual.stock_query: woman enjoying early evening dinner

scenes.narration: Third, your bed. The NHS suggests raising the head of the bed by around ten to twenty centimetres, so your chest and head are above your waist. That's roughly four to eight inches.

visual.stock_query: bed gently tilted, head end raised

scenes.narration: That means raising the bed itself, instead of adding pillows.

visual.stock_query: pillow pile crossed out, tilted bed

scenes.narration: Fourth, think about triggers. The NHS lists coffee, tomatoes, alcohol, chocolate and fatty or spicy foods as things that may trigger it for some people.

visual.quote: coffee, tomatoes, alcohol, chocolate and fatty or spicy foods
visual.stock_query: coffee cup, tomato, chocolate, chilli icons

scenes.narration: These aren't bad foods. They're just worth noticing. If chocolate sets you off and tomatoes don't, that's your answer, not anyone else's.

visual.stock_query: person writing in food notebook, smiling

scenes.narration: The NHS also suggests not wearing clothes that are tight around your waist, and not smoking.

visual.stock_query: comfy loose trousers on hanger

scenes.narration: Those are the NHS habits. But burping has its own sneaky culprit, and it isn't food at all. It's air.

visual.stock_query: cartoon air bubbles sneaking into mouth

scenes.narration: Fizzy drinks, chewing gum, drinking through a straw and eating fast may all mean swallowing extra air. Cutting back on them may help some people.

visual.stock_query: soda, gum, straw icons with bubbles

scenes.narration: And eating slowly may help on another front. Putting your fork down between bites gives you time to notice fullness before you're uncomfortably full.

visual.stock_query: person resting fork, relaxed meal

scenes.narration: Staying upright for a while after a meal, instead of lying on the sofa, is another simple step worth trying.

visual.stock_query: person on gentle evening walk

scenes.narration: One important note. If you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea, changes to how much or how often you eat matter more.

visual.stock_query: calm Medi mascot holding caution sign

scenes.narration: The label says using tirzepatide with those medicines may increase the risk of low blood sugar, including severe low blood sugar. So talk to your prescriber before changing your meal pattern.

visual.stock_query: person talking with prescriber, notepad

scenes.narration: And remember the stomach-emptying point? If you're thinking about a heartburn remedy from the pharmacy, ask the pharmacist which one suits you alongside tirzepatide and your other medicines.

factcheck.summary:
I checked every number and source-attributed claim against the live Zepbound prescribing information (Lilly, revised 8/2026), the DailyMed copy (updated 28 Aug 2026) and the NHS heartburn and acid reflux page (last reviewed 20 Nov 2023). They all match.
- **Label figures (Table 1, pooled Studies 1 and 2, adults with obesity or overweight, with or without type 2 diabetes, up to 72 weeks), placebo / 5 mg / 10 mg / 15 mg:**
  - Eructation (burping): 1% / 4% / 5% / 5%
  - Dyspepsia (indigestion): 4% / 9% / 9% / 10%
  - GERD (reflux): 2% / 4% / 4% / 5%
- **s15:** the "9 in 10" and "95 in 100" figures follow correctly from those numbers.
- **Label wording:** these lines match the label: the gastric-emptying line ("largest after the first dose… diminishes over time"), the nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea pattern during dose increases, the possible effect on absorption of oral medicines, the low-blood-sugar risk with insulin or sulfonylureas, and the pancreatitis and gallbladder signs from the Medication Guide.
- **NHS wording:** these match the page closely: smaller, more frequent meals; nothing within 3 or 4 hours before bed; raising the bed 10–20 cm and not using extra pillows; the exact trigger list; loose waistbands; not smoking; and the see-a-GP criteria.
- **Framing:** the mechanism is clearly hedged ("likely, not proven"). The script doesn't guess at what causes sulfur burps, says there is no set timeline for burping, and Dana is labelled as imagined.
- **Safety lines:** the don't-stop line is scoped to non-emergencies, and the disclaimer and prescriber lines are in order.

Only minor tagging and on-screen wording fixes remain.

issues.claim: Ask the pharmacist which heartburn remedy suits you alongside tirzepatide (tagged S1)
issues.problem: This pharmacist tip is our own advice. The label doesn't say it, so it shouldn't carry a source tag. The label backs only the absorption point, which s26 already cites.

issues.claim: Stat card: '~9 in 10' / 'No indigestion reported, tirzepatide 15 mg'
issues.problem: The muted-viewer test fails: the stat card doesn't say these are trial participants, and it gives no timeframe.
issues.fix: Set stat_label to: "Didn't report indigestion, tirzepatide 15 mg, 72-week trials"

issues.claim: pooled placebo-controlled trials lasting seventy-two weeks
issues.problem: The label describes the pooled trials as 'up to 72 weeks' of treatment. Both trials did run 72 weeks, so this is accurate, but the label's exact phrasing is safer.
issues.fix: Narration: "These figures come from pooled placebo-controlled trials of up to seventy-two weeks, in adults with obesity or overweight. Some of them also had type two diabetes."

issues.problem: GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease) is the long-term condition, not just acid reflux. The narration words it correctly, but the on-screen item is slightly looser.
issues.fix: Change the list item to "GERD = reflux disease (acid coming back up)"

thumbnail.reasoning:
Candidate #0 uses the state-change (worried face → calm face) layout, which is InforMed's proven top-performing thumbnail format (Side Effects hit 4.03% CTR with this exact layout) and is explicitly the default recommended by the growth playbook and performance notes. It reads instantly at both phone-feed and small sizes: bold white/yellow text with high contrast, one clear emotional before/after focal point (a distressed gray stomach turning into a smiling green one), and a simple 3-word headline. No clutter, no cut-off text, no overlapping elements.

Candidate #1 (big number) is legible and clean, but a sleepy cartoon stomach with "3-4 HRS" is a weaker emotional hook than a visible state change — it reads more like trivia than a promise of relief, likely lower CTR despite being perfectly legible.

Candidate #2 (pillow mistake) has a decent curiosity hook ("mistake" + red circle callout) but the focal hero is an inanimate bed with cartoon eyes rather than a relatable face, and the red circle (the "evidence" of the mistake) is small and could be missed at phone size. It's also a slightly more indirect connection to "burping," the title's lead symptom.

All three pass the ≥7 legibility bar and none are misleading relative to the title. Among them, #0 best matches the proven-performing format and carries the strongest emotional pull (worried → relieved), so it's the pick.
